idiom_name: FooBuilder with Option<T> fields, #[derive(Default)], fn x(mut self, ...) -> Self, build(self) -> Result<Foo, _>
implementation_notes: Rust requires every field at construction and has neither default arguments nor overloading, so builders are written by hand: a FooBuilder struct holding one Option<T> per optional setting (or the product itself with Option fields), #[derive(Default)], setters that take mut self and return Self - chaining moves the builder, and build(self) consuming it makes reuse after building a compile error - and a terminal build(self) -> Result<Foo, BuildError> that unwraps the required fields with an error naming the missing one. The standard library shows the shape (std::thread::Builder, std::process::Command, std::fs::OpenOptions), #[must_use] on the builder turns a forgotten .build() into a warning, and the derive_builder crate generates the same structure; prefer struct update syntax (Foo { a, ..Default::default() }) when every field has a sane default and nothing needs validating.
code_sketch:
let server = Server::builder(":8080")      // ServerBuilder, #[must_use]
    .read_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))
    .max_conns(1_000)
    .build()?;                             // Result<Server, BuildError>
// setters take `mut self` and return `Self`, so the chain moves the builder
pitfalls: Because setters consume the builder, a conditional step needs reassignment (b = b.timeout(d)); mixing a &mut self step into a consuming chain does not compile without care, so choose one ownership style.
A required field stored as Option<T> turns a missing value into a runtime Result/panic; #[must_use] plus an error naming the field keeps that honest, and the typestate builder removes it entirely.
Deriving Clone on the builder to "build twice" clones the whole accumulated state at every step, which is exactly what the consuming style avoids.

variants.name: Reusable &mut self builder
variants.idiom_name: setters fn x(&mut self) -> &mut Self with a repeatable build(&self)
variants.implementation_notes: Flipping the setters to &mut self keeps the builder usable as a named variable: steps can run in loops or under conditions without rebinding, and build(&self) can be called repeatedly to produce several products from one template (cloning or reconstructing the product each time). It costs a copy per built value and cannot be chained into a single expression unless the builder is bound first, so the consuming form stays the default for one-shot construction.
pitfalls: build(&self) must clone to hand out owned values, so building many products from one template pays a deep copy per product.
Nothing prevents reuse after build(), so any setter that consumes state (take()) silently empties the template for the next caller.
